notes.text: My life — It is my only request, that thou wouldst not give me up to the malice of that man who designs to take away my life. Even a stranger, a criminal, shall be permitted to petition for his life. But that a friend, a wife, a queen, should have occasion to make such a petition, was very affecting.

Sold — By the cruelty of that man who offered a great sum to purchase our destruction. Countervail - His ten thousand talents would not repair the king's loss, in the customs and tributes which the king receives from the Jews, within his dominions.

Who, &c. — The expressions are short and doubled, as proceeding from a discomposed and enraged mind. Durst - That is, to circumvent me, and procure a decree, whereby not only my estate should be so much impaired, and so many of my innocent subjects destroyed, but my queen also involved in the same destruction. We sometimes startle at that evil, which we ourselves are chargeable with. Ahasuerus is amazed at that wickedness, which he himself was guilty of. For he consented to the bloody edict. So that Esther might have said, Thou art the man!

Afraid — And it was time for him to fear, when the queen was his prosecutor, the king his judge, his own conscience a witness against him. And the surprising turns of providence that very morning, could not but increase his fear.

glossa.text:
« Harbona. » It signifies the doctors of the law, who foretold the crimes and the deceits of the Jews, whence Moses: « I know that after my death you will do wickedly, and will decline from the way which I have shown you ((Deut. XXXI)). » And in the Gospel: « There is one that accuseth you, Moses, in whom you trust ((Joan. V)). »

« In the house of Aman. » Aman signifies the wicked who raise tumult against Christ, and who persecute his Church. But Christ had been promised to them in the law; the law therefore, which was given for the keeping of life, was turned to death for them, by which they contrived to blot out Christ and to slay his confessors: and they who wished by the law to oppress the guiltless; that same law accusing them, received the sentence of a just judgment. They who have sinned in the law shall be punished by the law.

notes.text: The proud — Our enemies, compared to proud waters, for their great multitude and swelling rage. The safety of them that trust in God, and the fate of the wicked, ver. 1-5. A song of degrees.

glossa.text: *If it had not been that.* ((CASS.)) First the holy martyrs, mindful of how great things they have escaped, ascribe them to mercy alone; secondly, they give thanks that they have been delivered.

*Perhaps they had swallowed us up alive.* They live who know that an idol is nothing. They are dead who think it to be something. Therefore the dead are swallowed up, who think that the evil which they do is a thing to be done; but the living are they who indeed know that what they do is evil, but being overcome by persecution pass over into the fellowship of the ungodly, and prefer the sweetness of this life to God, as certain men did who for fear of death sacrificed to idols. ((AUG.)) Mark also that Peter, that is, the Church, swallows up many, but not alive. To whom it is said: *Slay and eat. ((Act. X.))* For he eats none, that is, sets none among his members, save one slain, that is, one renouncing the devil. He therefore is slain as to evil, but quickened as to good, who is eaten by Peter. The contrary befalls him whom the devil swallows down.

*Water.* ((AUG.)) The sinful people (and it is from the likeness of the Egyptians): which water flows as a torrent with violence, but quickly passes; whence he subjoins: *a torrent. --Perhaps* the Latins set down, as best they can, for the Greek ἄρα in the place of doubting, which is more intelligibly said: *thinkest thou, has our soul passed through?* that is, the greatness of the peril scarcely suffers this to be believed.
*Water insupportable.* ((AUG.)) Without substance, as are vices, and sins, and the sweetness of this life, etc., *as far as* and might bring back to the father the prodigal son worn out by long need.
*Blessed be the Lord.* ((CASS.)) The second part, where the saints give thanks that they have been delivered and that the snare has been broken.

*Our soul.* ((AUG.)) Or, as when someone makes a great noise, etc., *as far as* which is as it were a snare. *Of them that hunt.* ((ID.)) The hunters are the persecutors; the bait in the trap, the sweetness of this life. *The snare is broken.* ((CASS.)) The martyrs being slain, there remains no sweetness of life whereby they might be taken again: but they themselves were not broken along with it, nay rather delivered. *Broken.* ((ID.)) As if he should say: because it was of iron; not torn apart, like tow: so great was the fortitude of the passion, so great the power of him that delivered.

notes.text: Having anointed him with oil — This single conspicuous gift, which Christ committed to his apostles, Mark vi, 13, remained in the church long after the other miraculous gifts were withdrawn. Indeed, it seems to have been designed to remain always; and St. James directs the elders, who were the most, if not the only, gifted men, to administer at. This was the whole process of physic in the Christian church, till it was lost through unbelief. That novel invention among the Romanists, extreme unction, practiced not for cure, but where life is despaired of, bears no manner of resemblance to this.
And the prayer offered in faith shall save the sick — From his sickness; and if any sin be the occasion of his sickness, it shall be forgiven him.

Confess your faults — Whether ye are sick or in health. To one another - He does not say, to the elders: this may, or may not, be done; for it is nowhere commanded. We may confess them to any who can pray in faith: he will then know how to pray for us, and be more stirred up so to do. And pray one for another, that ye may be healed - Of all your spiritual diseases.
Elijah was a man of like passions — Naturally as weak and sinful as we are. And he prayed - When idolatry covered the land.
He prayed again — When idolatry was abolished.

As if he had said, I have now warned you of those sins to which you are most liable; and, in all these respects, watch not only over yourselves, but every one over his brother also. labour, in particular, to recover those that are fallen. If any one err from the truth — Practically, by sin.
He shall save a soul — Of how much more value than the body! ver. 14. And hide a multitude of sins - Which shall no more, how many soever they are, be remembered to his condemnation.

glossa.text: *Let him pray.* Let him not murmur, nor find fault with the judgments of God, but let him run to the Church with bended knees, that God may send consolation.
*And if he be in sins. ((BED.))* Many for their sins are punished even with the death of the body, etc., *as far as* whence it is rightly subjoined: *Confess ye,* etc.

*With prayer he prayed.* He proves by an example how much the constant supplication of a just man avails, since Elias, by praying with only one prayer, held back the heavens for so long a time, turned away the rains from the lands, denied fruits to mortals.

*And again. ((BED.))* When Elias saw the time, etc., *as far as* what then of many faithful men with many prayers?

*If any of you.* The efficacy of prayer being shown, he shows of how great merit it is to pray for the brethren, and to call them back to soundness, so that he who in the earlier part removed malignant and idle speech from our tongue, might show at the end of the Epistle what we ought to speak. Let us pray, and let us sing psalms, as often as we are beaten by adversities, let us confess our sins, let us pray for one another that we may be saved: for the salvation of our neighbours, not only the temporal, but rather the eternal. For if it be of great reward to snatch from death a body that must one day die, of how great merit is it to free from death a soul that shall live without end in the heavenly country?
*He shall save.* Certain codices have: *He shall save his own soul from death.* And truly he who corrects one that errs acquires for himself by this the ampler joys of the heavenly life.

notes.text: And John answered him — As if he had said, But ought we to receive those who follow not us? Master, we saw one casting out devils in thy name - Probably this was one of John the Baptist's disciples, who believed in Jesus, though he did not yet associate with our Lord's disciples. And we forbad him, because he followeth not us - How often is the same temper found in us? How readily do we also lust to envy? But how does that spirit become a disciple, much more a minister of the benevolent Jesus! St. Paul had learnt a better temper, when he rejoiced that Christ was preached, even by those who were his personal enemies. But to confine religion to them that follow us, is a narrowness of spirit which we should avoid and abhor. Luke ix, 49.

Jesus said — Christ here gives us a lovely example of candour and moderation. He was willing to put the best construction on doubtful cases, and to treat as friends those who were not avowed enemies. Perhaps in this instance it was a means of conquering the remainder of prejudice, and perfecting what was wanting in the faith and obedience of these persons. Forbid him not - Neither directly nor indirectly discourage or hinder any man who brings sinners from the power of Satan to God, because he followeth not us, in opinions, modes of worship, or any thing else which does not affect the essence of religion.

For he that is not against you, is for you — Our Lord had formerly said, he that is not with me, is against me: thereby admonishing his hearers, that the war between him and Satan admitted of no neutrality, and that those who were indifferent to him now, would finally be treated as enemies. But here in another view, he uses a very different proverb; directing his followers to judge of men's characters in the most candid manner; and charitably to hope that those who did not oppose his cause wished well to it. Upon the whole, we are to be rigorous in judging ourselves, and candid in judging each other.
For whosoever shall give you a cup — Having answered St. John, our Lord here resumes the discourse which was broken off at the 37th verse. Mark ix, 37. Matt. x, 42.
On the contrary, whosoever shall offend the very least Christian. Matt. xviii, 6; Luke xvii, 1.

And if a person cause thee to offend — (The discourse passes from the case of offending, to that of being offended) if one who is as useful or dear to thee as a hand or eye, hinder or slacken thee in the ways of God, renounce all intercourse with him. This primarily relates to persons, secondarily to things. Matt. v, 29; Matt. xviii, 8.

Where their worm — That gnaweth the soul, (pride, self will, desire, malice, envy, shame, sorrow, despair) dieth not - No more than the soul itself: and the fire (either material, or infinitely worse!) that tormenteth the body, is not quenched forever. Isaiah lxvi, 24.

Everyone — Who does not cut off the offending member, and consequently is cast into hell, shall be, as it were, salted with fire, preserved, not consumed thereby whereas every acceptable sacrifice shall be salted with another kind of salt, even that of Divine grace, which purifies the soul, (though frequently with pain) and preserves it from corruption.

Such salt is good indeed; highly beneficial to the world, in respect of which I have termed you the salt of the earth. But if the salt which should season others, have lost its own saltness, wherewith will ye season it? — Beware of this; see that ye retain your savour; and as a proof of it, have peace one with another. More largely this obscure text might be paraphrased thus:- As every burnt offering was salted with salt, in order to its being cast into the fire of the altar, so every one who will not part with his hand or eye, shall fall a sacrifice to Divine justice, and be cast into hell fire, which will not consume, but preserve him from a cessation of being. And on the other hand, every one, who, denying himself and taking up his cross, offers up himself as a living sacrifice to God, shall be seasoned with grace, which like salt will make him savoury, and preserve him from destruction forever. As salt is good for preserving meats, and making them savoury, so it is good that ye be seasoned with grace, for the purifying your hearts and lives, and for spreading the savour of my knowledge, both in your own souls, and wherever ye go. But as salt if it loses its saltness is fit for nothing, so ye, if ye lose your faith and love, are fit for nothing but to be utterly destroyed. See therefore that grace abide in you, and that ye no more contend, Who shall be greatest. Matt. v, 13; Luke xiv, 34.

glossa.text: *Forbid him not. ((BEDA.))* Hence the Apostle: *But whether by occasion or by truth Christ be preached,* etc., *as far as* we ought to detest and to forbid.

*And whosoever shall scandalize.* Although this be general, yet according to the sequence of the discourse it can be said against the apostles, who were disputing about the primacy and could destroy by their own example those whom they were calling to the faith. ((BEDA.)) Note that in our good work the scandal of a neighbour is sometimes to be guarded against, sometimes to be counted as nothing: in so far as we can without sin, we ought to avoid the scandal of our neighbours. But if scandal is taken for the sake of truth, it is more useful that it be suffered to arise than that the truth be forsaken.

*An ass's millstone. ((HIER.))* According to the custom of the province, etc., *as far as* a more tolerable punishment of hell would in any case torment him.

*And if it shall scandalize thee.* Because above he taught that we should not scandalize those who believe in him, he admonishes how much we ought to beware of those who scandalize. Σκάνδαλον in Greek is a stumbling-block, or a fall, or the striking of the foot. Or, as others say, a sharp stone. He therefore scandalizes his brother who by word or by deed affords him occasion of falling. *Thy hand.* A friend, of whose help and counsel we have need daily. But if he should be willing to wound us in the cause of the soul, he must be shut out from our fellowship, lest, if we will to have part with a lost man in this life, we perish together with him.

*Than having two hands. ((HIER.))* The two hands of princedom are humility and pride. Cut off pride; hold a humble princedom.

*Where the worm. ((BEDA.))* The stench of worms comes of the corruption of flesh and of blood; and therefore fresh meat is seasoned with salt, so that, the bloody humour being dried out, there can be no worm. Flesh therefore and blood breed worms, because carnal delight, which the seasoning of continence does not withstand, begets eternal punishment for the lustful. We ought therefore to chastise the body with the salt of continence, and the mind with the seasoning of wisdom, from the stain of error and of vices.

*For every one shall be salted with fire.* Because for the third time he made mention of fire and of the worm, he shows how we may be able to avoid both. *For every one with fire,* it is wondrously said: for what is salted with salt keeps off the rottenness of the worm. But what is salted with fire, that is, in fire, when salt has been sprinkled upon it, consumes the flesh as well. These things were done according to the law in the victims that were burned upon the altar, where it was commanded that salt be offered in every victim and sacrifice. *Every victim shall be salted with salt.* For he is truly a victim of the Lord who [offers] body and soul, etc., *as far as* to deny those dear and near to us. *Every victim shall be salted with salt. ((HIER.))* The victim is the human race, which here is salted with the salt of wisdom or of reason, while the corruption of blood, the keeper of rottenness and the mother of worms, is here consumed, and afterwards shall be tried by the fire of purgatory.

*But if the salt,* etc. That is, if a man once refreshed with the seasonings of truth return to apostasy: by what other teacher is he corrected, who has spat out the wisdom he tasted, either terrified by adversities or enticed by prosperity? Whence: *Who shall heal a charmer struck by a serpent? ((Eccli. XII.))* In this it is believed that Judas and his fellows are signified, who, corrupted by love of money, did not hesitate both to lose his apostleship and to betray the Lord. But because there are many whom, while greater knowledge lifts them up, it severs from the fellowship of others, and the more they savour, the more they lose their savour of the virtue of concord. He subjoins: *Have salt in you, and peace. ((BEDA.))* To have salt without peace is not the gift of virtue, but a proof of damnation. For the better a man savours, the worse he offends.

hymns.title: God, you are my refuge and my strength
Come, ye faithful, raise the strain
Come, Holy Ghost, our souls inspire

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: Elijah the Tishbite, who was of the foreigners of Gilead, said to Ahab, “As Yahweh, the God of Israel, lives, before whom I stand, there shall not be dew nor rain these years, but according to my word.”
echoes.note: 'Elijah… prayed earnestly that it might not rain, and it did not rain' draws directly on Elijah's word that 'there shall be neither dew nor rain these years, except by my word.' James reads the drought as answered prayer.

echoes.text: Elijah said to Ahab, “Get up, eat and drink; for there is the sound of abundance of rain.” So Ahab went up to eat and to drink. Elijah went up to the top of Carmel; and he bowed himself down on the earth, and put his face between his knees. He said to his servant, “Go up now, look toward the sea.” He went up, and looked, and said, “There is nothing.” He said, “Go again” seven times. On the seventh time, he said, “Behold, a small cloud, like a man’s hand, […]
echoes.note: 'He prayed again, and the sky gave rain' depends on Elijah on Carmel bowing to the ground in prayer until the rain came. The two-part drought-and-rain narrative is the backbone of James's example of the righteous person's prayer.

echoes.text: Hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all wrongs.
echoes.note: 'Love covers all offenses' stands behind 'he who turns a sinner… will cover a multitude of sins,' the proverb of love covering sin applied to restoring the wanderer.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s eyes are toward the righteous. His ears listen to their cry.
echoes.note: 'The eyes of the LORD are toward the righteous, and his ears toward their cry' grounds 'the insistent prayer of a righteous person is powerfully effective.'

echoes.text: The sacrifice made by the wicked is an abomination to Yahweh, but the prayer of the upright is his delight.
echoes.note: 'The prayer of the upright is acceptable to him' (cf. 15:29, 'he hears the prayer of the righteous') is the proverbial basis for the efficacy of the righteous person's prayer.

echoes.text: Also there arose Elijah the prophet as fire, And his word burned like a torch: Who brought a famine upon them, And by his zeal made them few in number. By the word of the Lord he shut up the heaven: Thrice did he thus bring down fire.
echoes.note: Ben Sira's praise of Elijah, who 'shut up the heavens' and 'brought down fire,' is the Second-Temple reception of the drought-prayer that James presupposes.

echoes.text: When I tell the wicked, O wicked man, you shall surely die, and you don’t speak to warn the wicked from his way; that wicked man shall die in his iniquity, but his blood will I require at your hand. Nevertheless, if you warn the wicked of his way to turn from it, and he doesn’t turn from his way; he shall die in his iniquity, but you have delivered your soul.
echoes.note: The watchman who warns the wicked to turn 'will have saved his life' is the prophetic logic behind saving a soul from death by turning the sinner back (cf. Ezekiel 3:18-21).

echoes.text: Those who are wise shall shine as the brightness of the expanse; and those who turn many to righteousness as the stars forever and ever.
echoes.note: 'Those who turn many to righteousness' shine like the stars — a faint echo behind turning a sinner from the error of his way.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: A young man ran, and told Moses, and said, “Eldad and Medad are prophesying in the camp!”
echoes.note: John's complaint about an outsider casting out demons in Jesus' name, and the demand to forbid him, closely parallels Joshua's plea that Moses forbid Eldad and Medad from prophesying outside the tent. Jesus' refusal to forbid mirrors Moses' magnanimous reply. The structural and thematic parallel is striking.

echoes.text: Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of Moses, one of his chosen men, answered, “My lord Moses, forbid them!”
echoes.note: Joshua's 'My lord Moses, forbid them' is answered by Moses' wish that all the LORD's people were prophets. Mark casts the disciples as Joshua and Jesus as the larger-hearted Moses who will not restrict the Spirit's work. The parallel reinforces the Moses typology running through the chapter.

echoes.text: Moses said to him, “Are you jealous for my sake? I wish that all Yahweh’s people were prophets, that Yahweh would put his Spirit on them!”
echoes.note: Moses' 'Would that all the LORD's people were prophets' anticipates Jesus' inclusive 'whoever is not against us is for us.' The generous expansion of authorized agency is shared. The echo completes the Eldad-and-Medad parallel.

echoes.text: “They shall go out, and look on the dead bodies of the men who have transgressed against me: for their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched; and they will be loathsome to all mankind.”
echoes.note: The thrice-repeated 'where their worm does not die, and the fire is not quenched' is a near-verbatim quotation of Isaiah's closing vision of the corpses of rebels, an undying worm and unquenchable fire. This is the strongest OT contact in the chapter and supplies the imagery of Gehenna. The repetition underscores the volume and centrality.

echoes.text: Every offering of your meal offering you shall season with salt; neither shall you allow the salt of the covenant of your God to be lacking from your meal offering. With all your offerings you shall offer salt.
echoes.note: 'Every sacrifice will be seasoned with salt' draws directly on the law that every grain offering be salted, never omitting the salt of the covenant. Mark's pairing of fire and salt with sacrifice reflects this cultic prescription. The verbal contact on salting the sacrifice is high.

echoes.text: All the wave offerings of the holy things, which the children of Israel offer to Yahweh, have I given you, and your sons and your daughters with you, as a portion forever. It is a covenant of salt forever before Yahweh to you and to your seed with you.”
echoes.note: The 'covenant of salt forever' between the LORD and the priests illuminates 'have salt in yourselves, and be at peace,' linking salt to enduring covenant fidelity. The covenant-of-salt motif undergirds the call to mutual peace. It strengthens the cultic-covenantal reading of the salt sayings.

echoes.text: Ought you not to know that Yahweh, the God of Israel, gave the kingdom over Israel to David forever, even to him and to his sons by a covenant of salt?
echoes.note: The kingship given to David by 'a covenant of salt' reinforces salt as a symbol of permanent covenant, supporting Jesus' exhortation to keep salt and peace. The contact is general and reinforcing. It corroborates the covenant-of-salt background.

echoes.text: You shall bring them near to Yahweh, and the priests shall cast salt on them, and they shall offer them up for a burnt offering to Yahweh.
echoes.note: The priests casting salt on the offerings before the LORD adds to the salted-sacrifice background of 9:49. The cultic salting of offerings coheres with Mark's 'every sacrifice salted with salt.' A reinforcing low-volume echo.

echoes.text: For his burning place has long been ready. Yes, for the king it is prepared. He has made its pyre deep and large with fire and much wood. Yahweh’s breath, like a stream of sulfur, kindles it.
echoes.note: Topheth prepared with fire and a great pile of wood, kindled by the breath of the LORD, contributes to the fiery-judgment imagery behind Gehenna and 'everyone salted with fire.' The link reinforces the burning-judgment theme. Volume is modest beside Isaiah 66.

echoes.text: They have built the high places of Topheth, which is in the valley of the son of Hinnom, to burn their sons and their daughters in the fire; which I didn’t command, nor did it come into my mind.
echoes.note: The valley of the son of Hinnom (Ge-Hinnom), site of child sacrifice condemned by Jeremiah, is the geographical and historical root of 'Gehenna.' Mark's term presupposes this defiled valley as the image of fiery judgment. The connection is etymological and background rather than a verbal citation.

echoes.text: therefore, behold, the days come, says Yahweh, that this place shall no more be called Topheth, nor The valley of the son of Hinnom, but The valley of Slaughter.
echoes.note: Jeremiah renames Topheth the 'valley of slaughter,' deepening the Hinnom-valley associations behind Gehenna. The judgment-in-the-valley motif underlies Mark's hell imagery. A reinforcing background echo.

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
echoes.note: The resurrection of some to everlasting contempt provides an apocalyptic frame for the unending punishment evoked by the undying worm and unquenchable fire. The shame-and-punishment of the wicked coheres with Mark's warnings. The contact is thematic and reinforces the Isaiah 66 quotation.

echoes.text: “Woe to the nations who rise up against my race! The Lord Almighty will take vengeance on them in the day of judgement, to put fire and worms in their flesh; and they will weep and feel their pain forever.”
echoes.note: Judith's hymn warns that the Lord will give fire and worms to the flesh of the nations, weeping in pain forever, a Second-Temple development of Isaiah 66:24. Its availability shows the worm-and-fire judgment circulating in the period Mark writes. It corroborates the deuterocanonical reception of the Isaiah imagery.

echoes.text: I will bring the third part into the fire, and will refine them as silver is refined, and will test them like gold is tested. They will call on my name, and I will hear them. I will say, ‘It is my people;’ and they will say, ‘Yahweh is my God.’”
echoes.note: Bringing the remnant through the fire to refine them lies faintly behind 'everyone will be salted with fire,' if the fire is read as purifying rather than only punitive. The refining-fire motif coheres with a disciple-formation reading of the saying. Low volume and contested.

notes.text: Israel also — Whose special relation and obligation to God should have restrained them from such carriage. Flesh - This word is here taken generally so as to include fish, as the next words shew. They had indeed cattle which they brought out of Egypt, but these were reserved for breed to be carried into Canaan, and were so few that they would scarce have served them for a month.

Freely — Either without price, for fish was very plentiful, and fishing was there free, or with a very small price. And this is the more probable because the Egyptians might not taste of fish, nor of the leeks and onions, which they worshipped for Gods, and therefore the Israelites, might have them upon cheap terms.

Our soul — Either our life, as the soul signifies, Gen. ix, 5, or our body, which is often signified by the soul. Dried away - Is withered and pines away; which possibly might be true, through envy and discontent, and inordinate appetite.
In the door of his tent — To note they were not ashamed of their sin.
Not found favour — Why didst thou not hear my prayer, when I desired thou wouldest excuse me, and commit the care of this unruly people to some other person.
Have I begotten them? — Are they my children, that I should be obliged to provide food and all things for their necessity and desire?

To bear — The burden of providing for and satisfying them. Alone - Others were only assistant to him in smaller matters; but the harder and greater affairs, such as this unquestionably was, were brought to Moses and determined by him alone.

My wretchedness — Hebrew. my evil, my torment, arising from the insuperable difficulty of my office and work of ruling this people, and from the dread of their utter extirpation, and the dishonour which thence will accrue to God and to religion, as if, not I only, but God also were an impostor.

To be elders — Whom thou by experience discernest to be elders not only in years, and name, but also in wisdom and authority with the people. And according to this constitution, the Sanhedrim, or great council of the Jews, which in after-ages sat at Jerusalem, and was the highest court of the judgment among them, consisted of seventy men.

Moses went out — Out of the tabernacle, into which he entered to receive God's answers from the mercy-seat. The seventy men - They are called seventy from the stated number, though two of them were lacking, as the Apostles are called the twelve, Matt. xxvi, 20, when one of that number was absent. Round the tabernacle - Partly that the awe of God might be imprinted upon their hearts, that they might more seriously undertake and more faithfully manage their high employment, but principally, because that was the place where God manifested himself, and therefore there he would bestow his spirit upon them.

Rested on them — Not only moved them for a time, but took up his settled abode with them, because the use and end of this gift was perpetual. They prophesied - Discoursed of the word and works of God in a marvelous manner, as the prophets did. So this word is used, 1 Sam. x, 5, 6 Joel ii, 28; 1 Cor. xiv, 3. Yet were they not hereby constituted teachers, but civil magistrates, who together with the spirit of government, received also the spirit of prophesy, as a sign and seal both to themselves and to the people, that God had called them to that employment. They did not cease - Either for that day, they continued in that exercise all that day, and, it may be, all the night too, as it is said of Saul, 1 Sam. xix, 24, or, afterwards also, to note that this was a continued gift conferred upon them to enable them the better to discharge their magistracy; which was more expedient for them than for the rulers of other people, because the Jews were under a theocracy or the government of God, and even their civil controversies were decided out of that word of God which the prophets expounded.

In the camp — Not going to the tabernacle, as the rest did, either not having seasonable notice to repair thither: or, being detained in the camp by sickness, or some urgent occasion, not without God's special providence, that so the miracle might be more evident. Were written - In a book or paper by Moses, who by God's direction nominated the fittest persons.
Told Moses — Fearing lest his authority should be diminished by their prophesying; and thereby taking authority to themselves without his consent.

One of his young men — Or, one of his choice ministers, which may be emphatically added, to note that even great and good men may mistake about the works of God. Forbid them - He feared either schism, or sedition, or that by their usurpation of authority, independently upon Moses, his power and esteem might be lessened.

Enviest thou for my sake — Art thou grieved because the gifts and graces of God are imparted to others besides me? Prophets - He saith prophets, not rulers, for that he knew was absurd and impossible. So we ought to be pleased, that God is glorified and good done, tho' to the lessening of our own honour.

glossa.text: *The melons and the leeks. ((GREG., lib. XX Moral., cap. 19.))* The minds of carnal men, for the love of the world, etc., *as far as* where they may groan carnally.

*Gather unto me seventy. ((GREG., lib. XXIX Moral., cap. 13.))* As for the most part young men are called, etc., *as far as* it is plain that the old age of the mind, not of the body, is to be chosen.
*Moses therefore came, and told the people the words of the Lord, gathering them. ((ORIG., Hom. 6 in Num.))* Another reading: Moses went out, he says, etc., *as far as* and the like, etc.

*Taking away of the spirit.* ((ID.)) It is not to be understood, etc., *as far as* and its origin received no loss from the derivation.

*Had rested.* ((ID.)) *And the spirit rested upon them, and they all prophesied,* etc. It is not read that the spirit rested, etc., *as far as* he set forth the praise of their life and their virtues.

((ORIG.)) *And the spirit rested in them, and they prophesied,* etc. The spirit works continually, etc., *as far as* nor is it fitting that the presence of the Holy Spirit be there.

*But there remained in the camp.* Not by negligence did the Lord command, but by the devotion of humility, judging themselves unworthy of the receiving of so great a gift: therefore God, the judge of hearts, judged them worthy, and showed it.

*Why, saith he, art thou jealous. ((GREG., lib. XXIII Moral., cap. 24.))* The devout mind of pastors, etc., *as far as* who did not envy the good that he had.

*A multitude of quails, who a little,* etc. ((RAB. in Num. )) The carnal people of the Jews, etc., *as far as But our conversation is in heaven ((II Cor. X))*.

notes.text: The law — The doctrine delivered to his church, whether by Moses, or by other prophets. Having discoursed hitherto of the glory of God shining forth in, the visible heavens, he now proceeds to another demonstration of God's glory, which he compares with and prefers before the former. Perfect - Completely discovering both the nature and will of God, and the whole duty of man, what he is to believe and practice, and whatsoever is necessary to his present and eternal happiness. Whereas the creation, although it did declare so much of God, as left all men without excuse, yet did not fully manifest the will of God, nor bring men to eternal salvation. Converting - From sin to God, from whom all men are naturally revolted. Testimony - His law, so called because it is a witness between God and man, what God requires of man, and what upon the performance of that condition, he will do for man. Sure - Hebrew. faithful or true, which is most necessary in a witness: it will not mislead any man, but will infallibly bring him to happiness. Simple - Even persons of the lowest capacities.

Right — Both in themselves, and in their effect, as guiding men in the ready way to eternal happiness. Rejoicing - By the discoveries of God's love to sinful men, in offers and promises of mercy. Commandment - All his commands. Pure - Without the least mixture of error. The eyes - Of the mind, with a compleat manifestation of God's will and man's duty: both which, the works of nature, and all the writings of men discover but darkly and imperfectly.

The fear — The law and word of God, because it is both the object and the rule, and the cause of holy fear. Clean - Sincere, not adulterated with any mixture. Constant and unchangeable, the same for substance in all ages. Judgments - God's laws are frequently called his judgments, because they are the declarations of his righteous will, and as it were his judicial sentence by which he expects that men should govern themselves, and by which he will judge them at the last day.

Who — Thy law, O Lord, is holy and just and good. But I fall infinitely short of it. Cleanse - Both by justification, through the blood of thy son; and by sanctification thro' thy Holy Spirit. Though the first may seem to be principally intended, because he speaks of his past sins. Secret - From the guilt of such sins as were secret either, from others; such as none knows but God and my own conscience: or, from myself; such as I never observed, or did not discern the evil of. Pardon my unknown sins, of which I never repented particularly, as I should have done.

Presumptuous — From known and evident sins, such as are committed against knowledge, against the checks of conscience, and the motions of God's spirit. Dominion - If I be at any time tempted to such sins, Lord let them not prevail over me, and if I do fall into them, let me speedily rise again.

Let — Having prayed that God would keep him from sinful actions, he now prays that God would govern, and sanctify his words and thoughts: and this was necessary to preserve him from presumptuous sins, which have their first rise in the thoughts. Redeemer - This expression seems to be added emphatically, and with special respect to Christ, to whom alone this word Goel can properly belong. A prayer for the king, ver. 1-4. The king and the people rejoice in God, and pray for his help, ver. 5-9. To the chief musician, A psalm of David.

glossa.text: *The law of the Lord.* ((CAS.)) Secondly, he praises the precepts of the New and the Old Testament. ((Ibid.)) The law given through Moses, correcting all things by the distinction of its words, and sending them on to the grace of Christ. *Converting.* ((AUG.)) By liberty, unto the imitating of himself, not pressing down with the yoke of servitude. *Souls.* Wills, not merely hands, as the Old Testament did. *The testimony.* Whatsoever *Quaecunquae* testimonies he gave to Israel are full of truth, and have given wisdom to the humble. *Wisdom:* concerning things divine.

*The justices of the Lord. ((Ibid.))* All are right in him, who taught not what he did not do, so that they who imitate them might rejoice in them, seeing they would do them freely with charity, not slavishly with fear. ((CASS.)) *Justices,* the law which justifies; whatsoever it commands is just.

*The fear of the Lord. ((Ibid.))* The fear of the world is not holy, because it is not profitable, and it changes with the times. *The fear of the Lord* is without any perturbation, because it is a love mingled with dread, because if it fears the judge, it knows him merciful. ((AUG.)) Fear, not that penal fear for earthly things, for love of which the soul is afraid, but the chaste fear whereby, the more it loves, the more it is wary of offending the bridegroom, and therefore it is not cast out, but abides. *Judgments.* The judgments of God need not another's authority.

*Desirable things. ((Ibid.))* Or, much to be desired, or much gold and stone; or much that is precious. Desirable above gold, etc., *as far as,* whose will he sets before his own, and they are sweeter than he himself is to himself. *Above gold,* that is, everything that is sought after, whether for riches, or for power, or for pleasure. *Honey.* The food of God is honey; that is, one now loosed from the world; and the honeycomb, that is, because he is still wrapped about, for whom there is need of the pressure of God's hand squeezing him out, that he may go into life.

*Who understandeth sins. ((Ibid.))* Thirdly he asks to be purged of vices, that he may be a worthy psalmist, to report these sacraments. To a mind that sees, truth is sweet, and judgments sweet; to one that does not see, what sweetness is there? But why is it not seen? Because of sins: nor is it any wonder: *For who understandeth sins?* ((CASS.)) *Sins:* all of them, for certain of them are known. *Mine* defile, *others'* afflict, and now spare, drive back the persuader. *From my secret ones.* He includes all sins under two heads, etc., *as far as* whereby man was seduced; and by consenting he made it his own. ((AUG.)) There is no greater sin than to apostatize from God, which is the beginning of pride: but pride is the beginning and the cause of all sin.

notes.text: Having anointed him with oil — This single conspicuous gift, which Christ committed to his apostles, Mark vi, 13, remained in the church long after the other miraculous gifts were withdrawn. Indeed, it seems to have been designed to remain always; and St. James directs the elders, who were the most, if not the only, gifted men, to administer at. This was the whole process of physic in the Christian church, till it was lost through unbelief. That novel invention among the Romanists, extreme unction, practiced not for cure, but where life is despaired of, bears no manner of resemblance to this.
And the prayer offered in faith shall save the sick — From his sickness; and if any sin be the occasion of his sickness, it shall be forgiven him.

Confess your faults — Whether ye are sick or in health. To one another - He does not say, to the elders: this may, or may not, be done; for it is nowhere commanded. We may confess them to any who can pray in faith: he will then know how to pray for us, and be more stirred up so to do. And pray one for another, that ye may be healed - Of all your spiritual diseases.
Elijah was a man of like passions — Naturally as weak and sinful as we are. And he prayed - When idolatry covered the land.
He prayed again — When idolatry was abolished.

As if he had said, I have now warned you of those sins to which you are most liable; and, in all these respects, watch not only over yourselves, but every one over his brother also. labour, in particular, to recover those that are fallen. If any one err from the truth — Practically, by sin.
He shall save a soul — Of how much more value than the body! ver. 14. And hide a multitude of sins - Which shall no more, how many soever they are, be remembered to his condemnation.

glossa.text: *Let him pray.* Let him not murmur, nor find fault with the judgments of God, but let him run to the Church with bended knees, that God may send consolation.
*And if he be in sins. ((BED.))* Many for their sins are punished even with the death of the body, etc., *as far as* whence it is rightly subjoined: *Confess ye,* etc.

*With prayer he prayed.* He proves by an example how much the constant supplication of a just man avails, since Elias, by praying with only one prayer, held back the heavens for so long a time, turned away the rains from the lands, denied fruits to mortals.

*And again. ((BED.))* When Elias saw the time, etc., *as far as* what then of many faithful men with many prayers?

*If any of you.* The efficacy of prayer being shown, he shows of how great merit it is to pray for the brethren, and to call them back to soundness, so that he who in the earlier part removed malignant and idle speech from our tongue, might show at the end of the Epistle what we ought to speak. Let us pray, and let us sing psalms, as often as we are beaten by adversities, let us confess our sins, let us pray for one another that we may be saved: for the salvation of our neighbours, not only the temporal, but rather the eternal. For if it be of great reward to snatch from death a body that must one day die, of how great merit is it to free from death a soul that shall live without end in the heavenly country?
*He shall save.* Certain codices have: *He shall save his own soul from death.* And truly he who corrects one that errs acquires for himself by this the ampler joys of the heavenly life.

notes.text: And John answered him — As if he had said, But ought we to receive those who follow not us? Master, we saw one casting out devils in thy name - Probably this was one of John the Baptist's disciples, who believed in Jesus, though he did not yet associate with our Lord's disciples. And we forbad him, because he followeth not us - How often is the same temper found in us? How readily do we also lust to envy? But how does that spirit become a disciple, much more a minister of the benevolent Jesus! St. Paul had learnt a better temper, when he rejoiced that Christ was preached, even by those who were his personal enemies. But to confine religion to them that follow us, is a narrowness of spirit which we should avoid and abhor. Luke ix, 49.

Jesus said — Christ here gives us a lovely example of candour and moderation. He was willing to put the best construction on doubtful cases, and to treat as friends those who were not avowed enemies. Perhaps in this instance it was a means of conquering the remainder of prejudice, and perfecting what was wanting in the faith and obedience of these persons. Forbid him not - Neither directly nor indirectly discourage or hinder any man who brings sinners from the power of Satan to God, because he followeth not us, in opinions, modes of worship, or any thing else which does not affect the essence of religion.

For he that is not against you, is for you — Our Lord had formerly said, he that is not with me, is against me: thereby admonishing his hearers, that the war between him and Satan admitted of no neutrality, and that those who were indifferent to him now, would finally be treated as enemies. But here in another view, he uses a very different proverb; directing his followers to judge of men's characters in the most candid manner; and charitably to hope that those who did not oppose his cause wished well to it. Upon the whole, we are to be rigorous in judging ourselves, and candid in judging each other.
For whosoever shall give you a cup — Having answered St. John, our Lord here resumes the discourse which was broken off at the 37th verse. Mark ix, 37. Matt. x, 42.
On the contrary, whosoever shall offend the very least Christian. Matt. xviii, 6; Luke xvii, 1.

And if a person cause thee to offend — (The discourse passes from the case of offending, to that of being offended) if one who is as useful or dear to thee as a hand or eye, hinder or slacken thee in the ways of God, renounce all intercourse with him. This primarily relates to persons, secondarily to things. Matt. v, 29; Matt. xviii, 8.

Where their worm — That gnaweth the soul, (pride, self will, desire, malice, envy, shame, sorrow, despair) dieth not - No more than the soul itself: and the fire (either material, or infinitely worse!) that tormenteth the body, is not quenched forever. Isaiah lxvi, 24.

Everyone — Who does not cut off the offending member, and consequently is cast into hell, shall be, as it were, salted with fire, preserved, not consumed thereby whereas every acceptable sacrifice shall be salted with another kind of salt, even that of Divine grace, which purifies the soul, (though frequently with pain) and preserves it from corruption.

Such salt is good indeed; highly beneficial to the world, in respect of which I have termed you the salt of the earth. But if the salt which should season others, have lost its own saltness, wherewith will ye season it? — Beware of this; see that ye retain your savour; and as a proof of it, have peace one with another. More largely this obscure text might be paraphrased thus:- As every burnt offering was salted with salt, in order to its being cast into the fire of the altar, so every one who will not part with his hand or eye, shall fall a sacrifice to Divine justice, and be cast into hell fire, which will not consume, but preserve him from a cessation of being. And on the other hand, every one, who, denying himself and taking up his cross, offers up himself as a living sacrifice to God, shall be seasoned with grace, which like salt will make him savoury, and preserve him from destruction forever. As salt is good for preserving meats, and making them savoury, so it is good that ye be seasoned with grace, for the purifying your hearts and lives, and for spreading the savour of my knowledge, both in your own souls, and wherever ye go. But as salt if it loses its saltness is fit for nothing, so ye, if ye lose your faith and love, are fit for nothing but to be utterly destroyed. See therefore that grace abide in you, and that ye no more contend, Who shall be greatest. Matt. v, 13; Luke xiv, 34.

glossa.text: *Forbid him not. ((BEDA.))* Hence the Apostle: *But whether by occasion or by truth Christ be preached,* etc., *as far as* we ought to detest and to forbid.

*And whosoever shall scandalize.* Although this be general, yet according to the sequence of the discourse it can be said against the apostles, who were disputing about the primacy and could destroy by their own example those whom they were calling to the faith. ((BEDA.)) Note that in our good work the scandal of a neighbour is sometimes to be guarded against, sometimes to be counted as nothing: in so far as we can without sin, we ought to avoid the scandal of our neighbours. But if scandal is taken for the sake of truth, it is more useful that it be suffered to arise than that the truth be forsaken.

*An ass's millstone. ((HIER.))* According to the custom of the province, etc., *as far as* a more tolerable punishment of hell would in any case torment him.

*And if it shall scandalize thee.* Because above he taught that we should not scandalize those who believe in him, he admonishes how much we ought to beware of those who scandalize. Σκάνδαλον in Greek is a stumbling-block, or a fall, or the striking of the foot. Or, as others say, a sharp stone. He therefore scandalizes his brother who by word or by deed affords him occasion of falling. *Thy hand.* A friend, of whose help and counsel we have need daily. But if he should be willing to wound us in the cause of the soul, he must be shut out from our fellowship, lest, if we will to have part with a lost man in this life, we perish together with him.

*Than having two hands. ((HIER.))* The two hands of princedom are humility and pride. Cut off pride; hold a humble princedom.

*Where the worm. ((BEDA.))* The stench of worms comes of the corruption of flesh and of blood; and therefore fresh meat is seasoned with salt, so that, the bloody humour being dried out, there can be no worm. Flesh therefore and blood breed worms, because carnal delight, which the seasoning of continence does not withstand, begets eternal punishment for the lustful. We ought therefore to chastise the body with the salt of continence, and the mind with the seasoning of wisdom, from the stain of error and of vices.

*For every one shall be salted with fire.* Because for the third time he made mention of fire and of the worm, he shows how we may be able to avoid both. *For every one with fire,* it is wondrously said: for what is salted with salt keeps off the rottenness of the worm. But what is salted with fire, that is, in fire, when salt has been sprinkled upon it, consumes the flesh as well. These things were done according to the law in the victims that were burned upon the altar, where it was commanded that salt be offered in every victim and sacrifice. *Every victim shall be salted with salt.* For he is truly a victim of the Lord who [offers] body and soul, etc., *as far as* to deny those dear and near to us. *Every victim shall be salted with salt. ((HIER.))* The victim is the human race, which here is salted with the salt of wisdom or of reason, while the corruption of blood, the keeper of rottenness and the mother of worms, is here consumed, and afterwards shall be tried by the fire of purgatory.

*But if the salt,* etc. That is, if a man once refreshed with the seasonings of truth return to apostasy: by what other teacher is he corrected, who has spat out the wisdom he tasted, either terrified by adversities or enticed by prosperity? Whence: *Who shall heal a charmer struck by a serpent? ((Eccli. XII.))* In this it is believed that Judas and his fellows are signified, who, corrupted by love of money, did not hesitate both to lose his apostleship and to betray the Lord. But because there are many whom, while greater knowledge lifts them up, it severs from the fellowship of others, and the more they savour, the more they lose their savour of the virtue of concord. He subjoins: *Have salt in you, and peace. ((BEDA.))* To have salt without peace is not the gift of virtue, but a proof of damnation. For the better a man savours, the worse he offends.

echoes.text: Elijah the Tishbite, who was of the foreigners of Gilead, said to Ahab, “As Yahweh, the God of Israel, lives, before whom I stand, there shall not be dew nor rain these years, but according to my word.”
echoes.note: 'Elijah… prayed earnestly that it might not rain, and it did not rain' draws directly on Elijah's word that 'there shall be neither dew nor rain these years, except by my word.' James reads the drought as answered prayer.

echoes.text: Elijah said to Ahab, “Get up, eat and drink; for there is the sound of abundance of rain.” So Ahab went up to eat and to drink. Elijah went up to the top of Carmel; and he bowed himself down on the earth, and put his face between his knees. He said to his servant, “Go up now, look toward the sea.” He went up, and looked, and said, “There is nothing.” He said, “Go again” seven times. On the seventh time, he said, “Behold, a small cloud, like a man’s hand, […]
echoes.note: 'He prayed again, and the sky gave rain' depends on Elijah on Carmel bowing to the ground in prayer until the rain came. The two-part drought-and-rain narrative is the backbone of James's example of the righteous person's prayer.

echoes.text: Hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all wrongs.
echoes.note: 'Love covers all offenses' stands behind 'he who turns a sinner… will cover a multitude of sins,' the proverb of love covering sin applied to restoring the wanderer.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s eyes are toward the righteous. His ears listen to their cry.
echoes.note: 'The eyes of the LORD are toward the righteous, and his ears toward their cry' grounds 'the insistent prayer of a righteous person is powerfully effective.'

echoes.text: The sacrifice made by the wicked is an abomination to Yahweh, but the prayer of the upright is his delight.
echoes.note: 'The prayer of the upright is acceptable to him' (cf. 15:29, 'he hears the prayer of the righteous') is the proverbial basis for the efficacy of the righteous person's prayer.

echoes.text: Also there arose Elijah the prophet as fire, And his word burned like a torch: Who brought a famine upon them, And by his zeal made them few in number. By the word of the Lord he shut up the heaven: Thrice did he thus bring down fire.
echoes.note: Ben Sira's praise of Elijah, who 'shut up the heavens' and 'brought down fire,' is the Second-Temple reception of the drought-prayer that James presupposes.

echoes.text: When I tell the wicked, O wicked man, you shall surely die, and you don’t speak to warn the wicked from his way; that wicked man shall die in his iniquity, but his blood will I require at your hand. Nevertheless, if you warn the wicked of his way to turn from it, and he doesn’t turn from his way; he shall die in his iniquity, but you have delivered your soul.
echoes.note: The watchman who warns the wicked to turn 'will have saved his life' is the prophetic logic behind saving a soul from death by turning the sinner back (cf. Ezekiel 3:18-21).

echoes.text: Those who are wise shall shine as the brightness of the expanse; and those who turn many to righteousness as the stars forever and ever.
echoes.note: 'Those who turn many to righteousness' shine like the stars — a faint echo behind turning a sinner from the error of his way.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: A young man ran, and told Moses, and said, “Eldad and Medad are prophesying in the camp!”
echoes.note: John's complaint about an outsider casting out demons in Jesus' name, and the demand to forbid him, closely parallels Joshua's plea that Moses forbid Eldad and Medad from prophesying outside the tent. Jesus' refusal to forbid mirrors Moses' magnanimous reply. The structural and thematic parallel is striking.

echoes.text: Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of Moses, one of his chosen men, answered, “My lord Moses, forbid them!”
echoes.note: Joshua's 'My lord Moses, forbid them' is answered by Moses' wish that all the LORD's people were prophets. Mark casts the disciples as Joshua and Jesus as the larger-hearted Moses who will not restrict the Spirit's work. The parallel reinforces the Moses typology running through the chapter.

echoes.text: Moses said to him, “Are you jealous for my sake? I wish that all Yahweh’s people were prophets, that Yahweh would put his Spirit on them!”
echoes.note: Moses' 'Would that all the LORD's people were prophets' anticipates Jesus' inclusive 'whoever is not against us is for us.' The generous expansion of authorized agency is shared. The echo completes the Eldad-and-Medad parallel.

echoes.text: “They shall go out, and look on the dead bodies of the men who have transgressed against me: for their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched; and they will be loathsome to all mankind.”
echoes.note: The thrice-repeated 'where their worm does not die, and the fire is not quenched' is a near-verbatim quotation of Isaiah's closing vision of the corpses of rebels, an undying worm and unquenchable fire. This is the strongest OT contact in the chapter and supplies the imagery of Gehenna. The repetition underscores the volume and centrality.

echoes.text: Every offering of your meal offering you shall season with salt; neither shall you allow the salt of the covenant of your God to be lacking from your meal offering. With all your offerings you shall offer salt.
echoes.note: 'Every sacrifice will be seasoned with salt' draws directly on the law that every grain offering be salted, never omitting the salt of the covenant. Mark's pairing of fire and salt with sacrifice reflects this cultic prescription. The verbal contact on salting the sacrifice is high.

echoes.text: All the wave offerings of the holy things, which the children of Israel offer to Yahweh, have I given you, and your sons and your daughters with you, as a portion forever. It is a covenant of salt forever before Yahweh to you and to your seed with you.”
echoes.note: The 'covenant of salt forever' between the LORD and the priests illuminates 'have salt in yourselves, and be at peace,' linking salt to enduring covenant fidelity. The covenant-of-salt motif undergirds the call to mutual peace. It strengthens the cultic-covenantal reading of the salt sayings.

echoes.text: Ought you not to know that Yahweh, the God of Israel, gave the kingdom over Israel to David forever, even to him and to his sons by a covenant of salt?
echoes.note: The kingship given to David by 'a covenant of salt' reinforces salt as a symbol of permanent covenant, supporting Jesus' exhortation to keep salt and peace. The contact is general and reinforcing. It corroborates the covenant-of-salt background.

echoes.text: You shall bring them near to Yahweh, and the priests shall cast salt on them, and they shall offer them up for a burnt offering to Yahweh.
echoes.note: The priests casting salt on the offerings before the LORD adds to the salted-sacrifice background of 9:49. The cultic salting of offerings coheres with Mark's 'every sacrifice salted with salt.' A reinforcing low-volume echo.

echoes.text: For his burning place has long been ready. Yes, for the king it is prepared. He has made its pyre deep and large with fire and much wood. Yahweh’s breath, like a stream of sulfur, kindles it.
echoes.note: Topheth prepared with fire and a great pile of wood, kindled by the breath of the LORD, contributes to the fiery-judgment imagery behind Gehenna and 'everyone salted with fire.' The link reinforces the burning-judgment theme. Volume is modest beside Isaiah 66.

echoes.text: They have built the high places of Topheth, which is in the valley of the son of Hinnom, to burn their sons and their daughters in the fire; which I didn’t command, nor did it come into my mind.
echoes.note: The valley of the son of Hinnom (Ge-Hinnom), site of child sacrifice condemned by Jeremiah, is the geographical and historical root of 'Gehenna.' Mark's term presupposes this defiled valley as the image of fiery judgment. The connection is etymological and background rather than a verbal citation.

echoes.text: therefore, behold, the days come, says Yahweh, that this place shall no more be called Topheth, nor The valley of the son of Hinnom, but The valley of Slaughter.
echoes.note: Jeremiah renames Topheth the 'valley of slaughter,' deepening the Hinnom-valley associations behind Gehenna. The judgment-in-the-valley motif underlies Mark's hell imagery. A reinforcing background echo.

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
echoes.note: The resurrection of some to everlasting contempt provides an apocalyptic frame for the unending punishment evoked by the undying worm and unquenchable fire. The shame-and-punishment of the wicked coheres with Mark's warnings. The contact is thematic and reinforces the Isaiah 66 quotation.

echoes.text: “Woe to the nations who rise up against my race! The Lord Almighty will take vengeance on them in the day of judgement, to put fire and worms in their flesh; and they will weep and feel their pain forever.”
echoes.note: Judith's hymn warns that the Lord will give fire and worms to the flesh of the nations, weeping in pain forever, a Second-Temple development of Isaiah 66:24. Its availability shows the worm-and-fire judgment circulating in the period Mark writes. It corroborates the deuterocanonical reception of the Isaiah imagery.

echoes.text: I will bring the third part into the fire, and will refine them as silver is refined, and will test them like gold is tested. They will call on my name, and I will hear them. I will say, ‘It is my people;’ and they will say, ‘Yahweh is my God.’”
echoes.note: Bringing the remnant through the fire to refine them lies faintly behind 'everyone will be salted with fire,' if the fire is read as purifying rather than only punitive. The refining-fire motif coheres with a disciple-formation reading of the saying. Low volume and contested.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Once Moses cried, Would that all the Lord's people were prophets, that God would put the Spirit on them all — and so God has, on you.
Have salt in yourselves, and be at peace.
A cup of water given in his name is not forgotten; even the smallest kindness is counted and kept.
Have salt in yourselves, and be at peace.
You are the salt that keeps the world from spoiling, the fire on the hearth that does not go out.
Have salt in yourselves, and be at peace.
So pray for one another, lift up the ones who are hurting, and come to worship the God who revives the soul.
Have salt in yourselves, and be at peace. Amen.
